Number theory

Source: vignettes/number-theory.Rmd
number-theory.Rmd

symcompR ports sympy.ntheory: primality testing and prime generation, integer factorization, arithmetic functions, modular arithmetic and residues, discrete logarithms, the Chinese remainder theorem, continued fractions, and partitions. Integers of any size are handled with the gmp package; pass a bigz (or a string) when a number does not fit in a double.

library(symcompR)
big <- function(s) gmp::as.bigz(s)

Primes

isprime() is a strong probable prime test that is deterministic for numbers below 2^{64} and has no known counterexample above it.

isprime(561)
#> [1] FALSE
isprime(big(2)^61 - 1)
#> [1] TRUE
isprime(big(2)^127 - 1)
#> [1] TRUE
is_mersenne_prime(127)
#> [1] TRUE
is_gaussian_prime(3 + 2 * sym_I)
#> [1] TRUE

561 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17 is the smallest Carmichael number: it fools the Fermat test for every base coprime to it, but not isprime().

is_carmichael(561)
#> [1] TRUE
is_fermat_pseudoprime(561, 2)
#> [1] TRUE

Generating primes:

nextprime(100)
#> [1] 101
prevprime(100)
#> [1] 97
prime(1000)
#> [1] 7919
primerange(50, 100)
#>  [1] 53 59 61 67 71 73 79 83 89 97
primepi(1000)
#> 168
primorial(5)
#> [1] 2310
mersenne_prime_exponent(10)
#> [1] 89

Factorization

factorint() returns the prime factorization as a named vector of exponents. It combines trial division, Pollard’s rho and p - 1 methods, and the elliptic curve method.

factorint(360)
#> 2 3 5 
#> 3 2 1
factorint(big(2)^64 - 1)
#>       3       5      17     257     641   65537 6700417 
#>       1       1       1       1       1       1       1
factorint(big(2)^67 - 1)
#>    193707721 761838257287 
#>            1            1
primefactors(360)
#> [1] 2 3 5
factorrat(Rational(-24, 35))
#> -1  2  3  5  7 
#>  1  3  1 -1 -1

2^{67} - 1 is the Mersenne number that Cole factored by hand in 1903. The individual methods are available too: pollard_rho(), pollard_pm1(), ecm() (elliptic curves), and qs() (the quadratic sieve).

pollard_rho(8051)
#> [1] 97
pollard_pm1(21477639576571, B = 2000)
#> [1] 4410317
ecm(big("398883434337287"))
#> [1]  4009823 99476569

Perfect powers and multiplicities:

perfect_power(6^5)
#> [1] 6 5
integer_nthroot(big(10)^40 + 1, 2)
#> $root
#> Big Integer ('bigz') :
#> [1] 100000000000000000000
#> 
#> $exact
#> [1] FALSE
multiplicity(2, 96)
#> [1] 5
multiplicity_in_factorial(2, 10)
#> [1] 8
smoothness(2^7 * 3^2)
#> [1]   3 128

Divisors and arithmetic functions 

divisors(60)
#>  [1]  1  2  3  4  5  6 10 12 15 20 30 60
divisor_count(60)
#> [1] 12
proper_divisors(28)
#> [1]  1  2  4  7 14
divisor_sigma(60)
#> 168
divisor_sigma(60, 2)
#> 5460
totient(60)
#> 16
reduced_totient(60)
#> 4
mobius(30)
#> -1
mobius(12)
#> 0
primenu(60)
#> 3
primeomega(60)
#> 4

totient(60) counts the integers below 60 coprime to it; reduced_totient() is the Carmichael function, the exponent of the multiplicative group modulo 60. These functions also accept symbols, and stay unevaluated:

n <- Symbol("n", integer = TRUE, positive = TRUE)
totient(n)
#> totient(n)

Perfect, abundant, and amicable numbers:

is_perfect(28)
#> [1] TRUE
abundance(12)
#> [1] 4
is_amicable(220, 284)
#> [1] TRUE

Modular arithmetic 

igcd(36, 48, 60)
#> [1] 12
ilcm(4, 6, 10)
#> [1] 60
mod_inverse(3, 11)
#> [1] 4
Integer(17) %% 5
#> 2

Chinese remainder theorem

crt(m, v) finds the x with x \equiv v_i \pmod{m_i}; it returns the solution and the modulus. solve_congruence() takes the pairs list(v, m) directly.

crt(c(3, 5, 7), c(2, 3, 2))
#> [1]  23 105
solve_congruence(list(2, 3), list(3, 5), list(2, 7))
#> [1]  23 105

This is the classic puzzle of Sunzi: a number that leaves remainders 2, 3, and 2 when divided by 3, 5, and 7 is 23 + 105k.

Residues and roots modulo n 

legendre_symbol(3, 7)
#> -1
jacobi_symbol(3, 35)
#> 1
quadratic_residues(11)
#> [1] 0 1 3 4 5 9
is_quad_residue(5, 11)
#> [1] TRUE
sqrt_mod(10, 13)
#> [1] 6
sqrt_mod(10, 13, all_roots = TRUE)
#> [1] 6 7
nthroot_mod(11, 3, 13, all_roots = TRUE)
#> numeric(0)

11 is not a cube modulo 13, so the last list is empty.

Orders, primitive roots, and discrete logarithms 

n_order(3, 7)
#> [1] 6
primitive_root(23)
#> [1] 5
is_primitive_root(5, 23)
#> [1] TRUE
discrete_log(41, 15, 7)
#> [1] 3

discrete_log(41, 15, 7) solves 7^k \equiv 15 \pmod{41}, giving k = 3.

Continued fractions

continued_fraction() expands a rational number or a quadratic irrational. The expansion of \sqrt{7} is periodic: the second element is the repeating block.

continued_fraction(Rational(415, 93))
#> [1] 4 2 6 7
continued_fraction(sqrt(S(7)))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 1 1 1 4
continued_fraction_periodic(0, 1, 7)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 1 1 1 4
continued_fraction_reduce(c(4, 2, 6, 7))
#> 415/93
continued_fraction_iterator(sym_pi, 6)
#> [1]   3   7  15   1 292   1
continued_fraction_convergents(c(3, 7, 15, 1, 292))
#> [[1]]
#> 3
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 22/7
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> 333/106
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> 355/113
#> 
#> [[5]]
#> 103993/33102

The convergents of \pi include the famous approximations 22/7 and 355/113.

egyptian_fraction() writes a rational number as a sum of distinct unit fractions:

egyptian_fraction(Rational(4, 13))
#> [1]   4  18 468

so 4/13 = 1/4 + 1/18 + 1/468.

egypt_harmonic() writes a rational number as a sum of the first terms of the harmonic series and a remainder:

egypt_harmonic(Rational(5, 2))
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[1]][[2]]
#> 2
#> 
#> [[1]][[3]]
#> 3
#> 
#> [[1]][[4]]
#> 4
#> 
#> [[1]][[5]]
#> 5
#> 
#> [[1]][[6]]
#> 6
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 1/20
egypt_harmonic(Rational(1, 3))
#> [[1]]
#> list()
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 1/3

Partitions and digits

npartitions() counts the partitions of an integer with the Hardy-Ramanujan-Rademacher formula, so large arguments are fast.

npartitions(100)
#> [1] 190569292
npartitions(1000)
#> Big Integer ('bigz') :
#> [1] 24061467864032622473692149727991
digits(123, 10)
#> [1] 10  1  2  3
digits(255, 16)
#> [1] 16 15 15
count_digits(1122334)
#> 1 2 3 4 
#> 2 2 2 1
is_palindromic(12321)
#> [1] TRUE
pi_hex_digits(0, 20)
#> [1] "3243f6a8885a308d3131"

digits() returns the base followed by the digits. pi_hex_digits() uses the Bailey-Borwein-Plouffe formula to compute hexadecimal digits of \pi starting at any position, without computing the earlier ones.

Integer sequences

The classical combinatorial numbers are functions that evaluate for integer arguments and stay symbolic otherwise.

fibonacci(50)
#> 12586269025
lucas(20)
#> 15127
catalan(10)
#> 16796
bell(10)
#> 115975
bernoulli(10)
#> 5/66
euler(10)
#> -50521
harmonic(10)
#> 7381/2520
partition(100)
#> 190569292
fibonacci(n)
#> fibonacci(n)

Sieves

sieve is a shared, growing table of primes, totients, and Möbius values. Sieve() creates a fresh one.

s <- Sieve()
s
#> prime sieve (6): 2, 3, 5, ... 11, 13
#> totient sieve (6): 0, 1, 1, ... 2, 4
#> mobius sieve (6): 0, 1, -1, ... 0, -1
class(sieve)
#> [1] "Sieve"

More primality tests

The probable prime tests behind isprime() are available individually: Miller-Rabin with given bases (mr()), the Lucas tests, the Euler and Euler-Jacobi tests, and Proth’s test for numbers k 2^n + 1.

mr(1373651, c(2, 3))
#> [1] FALSE
mr(1373653, c(2, 3))
#> [1] TRUE
is_lucas_prp(989)
#> [1] FALSE
is_strong_lucas_prp(5459)
#> [1] TRUE
is_extra_strong_lucas_prp(989)
#> [1] TRUE
is_euler_pseudoprime(341, 2)
#> [1] TRUE
is_euler_jacobi_pseudoprime(561, 2)
#> [1] TRUE
proth_test(41)
#> [1] TRUE
find_first_n_carmichaels(3)
#> [1]  561 1105 1729
find_carmichael_numbers_in_range(1, 3000)
#> [1]  561 1105 1729 2465 2821
carmichael$is_carmichael(561)
#> [1] TRUE
composite(1)
#> [1] 4
composite(1000)
#> [1] 1197
compositepi(100)
#> [1] 74
p <- randprime(1000, 2000)
isprime(p) && p >= 1000 && p < 2000
#> [1] TRUE

More divisor functions

Unitary divisors d of n have \gcd(d, n/d) = 1, and the antidivisors of n are the numbers that do not divide n by the largest possible margin.

udivisors(60)
#> [1]  1  3  4  5 12 15 20 60
udivisor_count(120)
#> [1] 8
udivisor_sigma(18, 3)
#> 6570
antidivisors(24)
#> [1]  7 16
antidivisor_count(24)
#> [1] 2
proper_divisor_count(12)
#> [1] 5
is_abundant(12)
#> [1] TRUE
is_deficient(13)
#> [1] TRUE
dra(19, 12)
#> [1] 8
drm(277777788888899, 10)
#> [1] 0
core(24)
#> [1] 6
core(64, 3)
#> [1] 1

core(n, t) is the t-th power free part of n: 24 is 2^2 \cdot 6, so its square free part is 6.

smoothness_p() reports, for each prime factor p of n, how smooth p - 1 (or p + 1 with m = 1) is; this decides how well the Pollard p - 1 and Williams p + 1 methods work.

smoothness_p(10431, m = 1)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> [1] 3 2 2 4
#> 
#> [[2]][[2]]
#> [1] 19  1  5  5
#> 
#> [[2]][[3]]
#> [1] 61  1 31 31

More modular arithmetic

crt1() and crt2() split the Chinese remainder computation into a precomputation that depends only on the moduli and a cheap second step. symmetric_residue() is the residue closest to zero, sqrt_mod_iter() iterates over square roots, and kronecker_symbol() extends the Jacobi symbol to all integers.

pre <- crt1(c(18, 42, 6))
crt2(c(18, 42, 6), c(0, 0, 0), pre[[1]], pre[[2]], pre[[3]])
#> [1]    0 4536
symmetric_residue(5, 7)
#> [1] -2
unlist(sqrt_mod_iter(11, 43))
#> [1] 21 22
kronecker_symbol(3, 8)
#> -1
is_nthpow_residue(2, 3, 7)
#> [1] FALSE
quadratic_congruence(2, 5, 3, 7)
#> [1] 2 6
polynomial_congruence("x^6 - 2*x^5 - 35", 6125)
#> [1] 3257
binomial_mod(10, 2, 6)
#> [1] 3

cycle_length() finds the tail length \mu and cycle length \lambda of the sequence x_{k+1} = f(x_k) with Brent’s algorithm:

cycle_length(function(x) (x^2 + 12) %% 17, 4)
#> $lambda
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $mu
#> [1] 0

Binomial and multinomial coefficients 

binomial_coefficients_list(5)
#> [1]  1  5 10 10  5  1
binomial_coefficients(3)
#> 0,3 1,2 2,1 3,0 
#>   1   3   3   1
multinomial_coefficients(3, 2)
#> 0,0,2 0,1,1 0,2,0 1,0,1 1,1,0 2,0,0 
#>     1     2     1     2     2     1
multinomial_coefficients_iterator(2, 3)
#> 0,3 1,2 2,1 3,0 
#>   1   3   3   1

Factoring with the quadratic sieve

qs() is the self-initializing quadratic sieve, with a bound on the factor base and a sieve interval; it returns the factors it finds, and qs_factor() returns them with their multiplicities. FactorCache() creates a cache of factorizations, and factor_cache is the cache that factorint() uses.

qs(10009202107, 100, 10000)
#> [1] 100043 100049
qs_factor(10009202107, 100, 10000)
#> 100043 100049 
#>      1      1
fc <- FactorCache(maxsize = 10)
class(fc)
#> [1] "FactorCache"
class(factor_cache)
#> [1] "FactorCache"

Points on elliptic curves

EllipticCurvePoint() creates a point in projective coordinates. point_order() finds the order of a point; on y^2 = x^3 + 1 the rational torsion group is cyclic of order 6.

E <- EllipticCurve(0, 1)
point_order(E$point(2, 3))
#> [1] 6
point_order(E$point(0, 1))
#> [1] 3
point_order(E$point(-1, 0))
#> [1] 2
EllipticCurvePoint(2, 3, 1, E)
#> (2, 3)
